preamble: The voiced alveolar sibilant [z] is replaced by the voiced dental non-sibilant fricative [ð], a dentalization in which the grooved sibilant becomes a flat interdental or dental fricative, usually alongside the parallel s > θ. Bashkir and Turkmen did this independently: both have [ð] where Common Turkic and their nearest relatives have z. In Iran, some reciters of Zoroastrian Persian songs pronounce /z/ as [ð].

examples.note: Bashkir has [ð] where Turkic generally has z, outside word-initial position (also оҙон 'long', Turkish uzun); Bashkir likewise turned s into [θ].
Unlike the other Oghuz languages, Turkmen realizes Common Turkic /z/ and /s/ as the dental fricatives [ð] and [θ], and has no /z/ or /s/ phonemes.
Recorded in Yazdi Zoroastrian oral poetry: a number of reciters have [θ] for /s/ and some [ð] for /z/; local Yazdi Persian shows s > [θ] but not z > [ð]. The feature is confined to some speakers.

sources: Bernard, C. (2020). A newly discovered Persian variety: the case of “Zoroastrian Persian”. Orientalia Suecana, 69, 57–67. https://doi.org/10.33063/diva-421118
